traveler: Jaufre Rudel, prince of Blaye (Joffrey Rudel)
title: Amor de Lonh: the Prince of Blaye, the Countess He Never Saw, and the Sea That Was Never Attested
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Angouleme, the cadet son who carries away the name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1047 is the death year of Geoffroi Taillefer, whose comital reign ran 1031 to 1047; the descent is genealogy printed in a tertiary source, not charter evidence
stops.campa: Geoffroi Taillefer, count of Angouleme since 1031, dies. A younger son of his carries the byname Rudel out of the comital house and down the river to a cadet holding on the Gironde. He is the great-grandfather of the poet. The counts of Angouleme and the counts of Poitou will spend the next hundred years disputing which of them Blaye answers to, and the family that took its name from a nickname holds the rock between the two of them, collecting what the estuary carries up toward Bordeaux and down toward the sea.
suggested_refs: The comital genealogy of Angouleme, Taillefer line, as relayed by fr.wikipedia after Poull-type reconstructions

stops.name: Blaye, the charter that says prince
stops.date_confidence: attested: the hardest document in the dossier; whether Girard is the poet's father or grandfather is disputed and left open
stops.campa: A charter names Girard I Rudel, castellan of the rock above the Gironde, and gives him a title larger than his holding: prince of Blaye. His own father is said to have taken that style around 1090. Blaye is a river gate and a customs post a few hours downstream of Bordeaux, and the men who hold it take a cut of everything that passes. This charter is the single hard document in the whole Rudel file. Everything else comes from six or seven poems, a biography written a century late, and genealogists working backward.
suggested_refs: The 1106 Blaye charter naming Girard I Rudel as prince, cited in reference works but not consulted directly
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Jaufre Rudel', citing charter evidence

stops.name: Blaye, birth on the estuary
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: French sources give 'vers 1110', others 1100 or 1113; English reference works decline the decade and give only 'early to mid-twelfth century'
stops.campa: Jaufre Rudel is born at Blaye, where the Gironde is wide enough to be taken for the sea. The town already carries other men's endings: Charlemagne is said to have laid Roland, Oliver and Turpin in white sarcophagi in the basilica of Saint-Romain here, and pilgrims on the Compostela road turn aside to stand over them. The boy born on this rock will be given no tomb at all. Blaye holds no grave of his and no stone with his name on it; the citadel standing there now is Vauban's, raised five hundred years after him.
suggested_refs: The ruined basilica of Saint-Romain at Blaye, and the absence of any Rudel monument in the town
sources: UNESCO Vauban fortifications file, Blaye citadel

stops.name: Bordeaux, the cathedral upstream
stops.date_confidence: context only: Blaye falls within the archdiocese and ducal orbit of Bordeaux, but no source records Rudel in the city
stops.campa: Blaye belongs to the archdiocese of Bordeaux and to the ducal orbit of Aquitaine, and Saint-Andre is the church its lords answer to. The whole political weather of Rudel's life is made here and at Poitiers, in the question of whose vassal Blaye is and whose coin runs in it. No document places him inside this cathedral or anywhere else in Bordeaux. The pin marks the authority above him rather than a visit. His life has almost no attested locations and this is one of the empty ones.
suggested_refs: Cathedrale Saint-Andre de Bordeaux, metropolitan church of the archdiocese covering Blaye
sources: Regional ecclesiastical geography of Gascony; no Rudel-specific document

stops.name: La Sauve-Majeure, a charter no one can produce
stops.date_confidence: unsourced: the research pool reported a 1125 abbey charter witnessed by a Jaufre Rudel de Blaye, but no reachable cartulary corroborates it; the charter consistently cited in the literature is the 1106 one naming Girard
stops.campa: The Benedictine abbey in the forest east of Bordeaux keeps a cartulary, and somewhere in the scholarship a 1125 act is said to carry a Jaufre Rudel de Blaye among its witnesses. It would be the closest thing to a documentary sighting of a man of this name and generation. Verification could not find it in any source reachable, and the philologists who mention such a witness cannot agree whether he would be the poet, his father, or a kinsman with the same name. The stop is here to hold the place of a document, not to report one.
suggested_refs: The cartulary of La Sauve-Majeure, Gironde: the 1125 act remains to be located and read
sources: Alfred Jeanroy, Les chansons de Jaufre Rudel (1915), as reported at second hand; identification treated as unproven

stops.name: Blaye, vested by the count of Angouleme
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wulgrin II of Angouleme reclaimed Blaye from William X of Aquitaine in 1127 and, the source says, 'probably' vested Jaufre with it; a rival hypothesis making Wulgrin his father is called flimsy by the same source
stops.campa: Wulgrin II of Angouleme takes the fortress of Blaye back from William X of Aquitaine, and probably puts Jaufre Rudel into it. The word probably belongs to the record and stays there. Older accounts date the transfer to 1130 and name the losing duke William VIII of Poitou, which is the Poitiers numbering for the same William X and has sent readers eighty years astray. The poet enters history as a piece in someone else's border quarrel: a prince by title and a tenant in fact, holding a rock that two counts want.
suggested_refs: The Angouleme-Poitou dispute over the suzerainty of Blaye, 1120s to 1140s

stops.name: Poitiers, the court that is only a guess
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a correction: the pool put him at William IX's court in the 1120s, impossible since William IX died in February 1126; the defensible milieu is William X's court of the 1130s and 1140s, and even that places him nowhere by document
stops.campa: The palace of the counts of Poitou and dukes of Aquitaine is where the new art is made. William IX, the first troubadour, is already dead; his son William X keeps the court, and Cercamon and Marcabru sing in it. Scholarship sets Rudel loosely in this light. Nothing puts him in the room. No charter witnesses him at Poitiers, and no poem of his or of anyone else's says he was ever there. He is placed at this court the way a star is placed by the light around it, by inference from the company he keeps in the manuscripts.
suggested_refs: The Palais des comtes de Poitou at Poitiers, court of William X
sources: General troubadour scholarship, Jeanroy 1915 and Rita Lejeune, at second hand

stops.name: Blaye, six songs, or seven
stops.date_confidence: corpus attested, count disputed: editors give six or seven cansos, four of them with musical notation; the composition years are unrecorded and 1140 sits inside the floruit as a placeholder
stops.campa: The whole surviving work of Jaufre Rudel is six poems, or seven, depending which editor is counting. Four of them come down with their music. Editors who have spent careers on the corpus describe it as difficult to interpret. The songs are built around a love that is defined by distance and never given a name or an address. Amor de lonh, love from far off. Out of that phrase, and nothing else, a biography will later be manufactured and believed for eight hundred years.
suggested_refs: The six or seven cansos of Jaufre Rudel, four with melodies, in the Occitan chansonnier tradition

stops.name: Blaye, when the days are long in May
stops.date_confidence: undatable: the cansos carry no dates and cannot be ordered; the year is a placeholder inside the floruit
stops.campa: The best known of the songs opens on a season and turns immediately away from it. The days lengthen, the birdsong from far away is sweet to him, and having left that place he remembers a love from far away. Nothing in the poem names a woman, a country, or a voyage. It is a grammar of longing rather than a report of one. Fifty years after his death a German will build a crusading song on this stanza; Walther von der Vogelweide takes the far love east with him, and the phrase outlives every fact anyone can establish about the man who wrote it.
stops.quote: Lanquan li jorn son lonc e May, M'es belhs dous chans d'auzelh de lonh, E quan mi suy partitz de lay, Remembra'm d'un'amor de lonh.
stops.quote_source: Jaufre Rudel, canso 'Lanquan li jorn son lonc en mai', Occitan text as transmitted, quoted in the Italian Wikipedia article 'Jaufré Rudel'; not collated against Jeanroy's 1915 critical edition
suggested_refs: 'Lanquan li jorn son lonc en mai' with its melody, and Walther von der Vogelweide's crusade song built on it

stops.name: Blaye, when the stream of the fountain clears
stops.date_confidence: undatable: no canso of Rudel can be dated; the year is a placeholder inside the floruit
stops.campa: A second canso begins with water running clear again as it does each year, the season turning over, and moves from that ordinary clearing into the same distance as the first. This is the other poem the reference works name when they explain amor de lonh. The two of them together are the entire evidentiary basis for the legend that follows: a lord on an estuary writing about a woman at an unstated remove, in a form where the beloved is conventionally unnamed anyway. The vida will read the convention as a biography.
stops.quote: Quan lo rius de la fontana S'esclarzis, si cum far sol
stops.quote_source: Jaufre Rudel, canso 'Quan lo rius de la fontana', Occitan, quoted in the French Wikipedia article 'Jaufré Rudel'
suggested_refs: 'Quan lo rius de la fontana', second of the two cansos cited for the amor de lonh theme

stops.name: Blaye, waking and then dreaming
stops.date_confidence: undatable, and textually uncertain: the reading 'somphnan' as printed looks like a transcription slip for 'sompnhan' or 'sompnan', dreaming; the error is left standing rather than silently mended
stops.campa: In a third song the far love follows him across the border between waking and sleep: he is troubled by it awake, and then dreaming, asleep. The line survives in a spelling that is probably wrong. What comes down is somphnan where the language wants sompnhan, one scribe's slip or one editor's, repeated forward into every quotation since. Nothing of his is in his own hand, and every word attributed to him has passed through a copyist a century after he died.
stops.quote: D'quest amor suy cossiros, Vellan e pueys somphnan dormen
stops.quote_source: Jaufre Rudel, stanza from 'Quan lo rossinhols el folhos', Occitan as printed in the French Wikipedia article 'Jaufré Rudel'; the spelling 'somphnan' is flagged as a probable transcription slip and left uncorrected
suggested_refs: 'Quan lo rossinhols el folhos', and the textual state of the Rudel corpus in the chansonniers

segments.name: The Countess of Tripoli, Who Is Never Named

stops.name: Edessa, the third daughter is born
stops.date_confidence: attested with corrected place: born c.1115 to 1117 in the County of Edessa, not in the Kingdom of Jerusalem; Baldwin of Bourcq was count of Edessa from 1100 and became king only on 2 April 1118
stops.campa: Hodierna is born to Baldwin of Bourcq and Morphia of Melitene, third of four daughters, in the county her father governs in the far north of the crusader states. Her sisters are Melisende, who will be queen of Jerusalem, and Alice. Only the youngest, Ioveta, will be born in the purple, after their father takes the throne in 1118. Hodierna is not yet the countess of Tripoli and never will be the woman of the poem; she is the woman later readers will decide the poem was about, which is not the same thing.
suggested_refs: The Edessan period of Baldwin of Bourcq, 1100 to 1118, and the births of his first three daughters

stops.name: Tripoli, a child promised to the count's heir
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Kevin Lewis calls a betrothal to Raymond II around 1122 'very possible'; the pool's 1127 is five years off
stops.campa: A betrothal is arranged, very possibly this year, between the king's daughter and Raymond, heir to the county of Tripoli. She is six or seven. The county is a strip of coast and mountain between Antioch and the kingdom, held from a citadel that Raymond of Saint-Gilles raised on the hill above the harbor forty years before. Everything about her life that the sources record is dynastic: a birth in Edessa, a betrothal here, a marriage delayed, a regency, a day of death without a year attached to it.
suggested_refs: The Citadel of Raymond de Saint-Gilles, Qal'at Sanjil, seat of the counts of Tripoli
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Hodierna of Tripoli', citing Kevin Lewis

stops.name: Tripoli, the marriage held back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Lewis presumes the marriage delayed to c.1132 because she was too young earlier; the pool's 1130 is unsupported
stops.campa: Hodierna marries Raymond II and becomes countess of Tripoli, the title under which she will be conscripted, a century later, into somebody else's love story. The marriage is presumed to have waited until now on account of her age. The county she enters is at the seam of the Frankish east, quarreling with Antioch on one side and with the kingdom on the other, and its countess is a king's daughter and a queen's sister, which is why she is worth marrying and why the legend will find her worth borrowing.
suggested_refs: The marriage of Hodierna of Jerusalem and Raymond II of Tripoli, c.1132
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Hodierna of Tripoli', citing Kevin Lewis

stops.name: Acre, first sighting of her in the record
stops.date_confidence: attested: December 1138, her first hard attestation as countess, at the court of Fulk and Melisende
stops.campa: The countess of Tripoli attends the court of King Fulk and her sister Queen Melisende at Acre. This is the first time a document actually shows her holding the title. The port is the main gate of the Frankish east; everything western arrives through it. Fifty-three years later Richard the Lionheart will spend two years and an army taking this same harbor back, and knight a Muslim boy called al-Kamil on its shore. For now it is a court in December, and a woman is present at it who has not yet been made famous by a poem she never read.
suggested_refs: The court of Fulk and Melisende at Acre, December 1138

stops.name: Vezelay, the sermon on the hill
stops.date_confidence: attested: Bernard preaches at Vezelay on 31 March 1146 and the king and queen take the cross there; the army departs Metz in June 1147, and the pool's collapsing of both into 1147 is a year late for the vow
stops.campa: Bernard of Clairvaux preaches the Second Crusade on the hill at Vezelay, and the crowd is so large the sermon is given outdoors. Louis VII takes the cross, and Eleanor of Aquitaine with him: granddaughter of William IX, the first troubadour, carrying the new art into a war. If Rudel's vow belongs to any wave it belongs to this one. Nothing places him at Vezelay or at Metz when the host marches fifteen months later, and no chronicle of the expedition names him at all.
suggested_refs: The hill of Vezelay, 31 March 1146, and Odo of Deuil's account of the departure
sources: Vida of Jaufre Rudel; Odo of Deuil, De profectione Ludovici VII in orientem, at second hand

stops.name: Blaye, the tornada that says oltra mar
stops.date_confidence: the reference is repeated everywhere, the poem carrying it is not securely identified: the pool assigned it to 'Pax in nomine Domini', which is Marcabru's Reconquista song about Spain; the standard editions put the Rudel tornada in 'Cortesamen vuoill comensar' (PC 293.15), unverified against a primary text
stops.campa: Marcabru, singing in Occitania, sends a song after Jaufre Rudel oltra mar, across the sea. Those two words are the only evidence outside the legend that a real man of this name went east, and they are the reason his death is dated at all. The pin is set at the seat he has left, because the song is sung here and he is not. Which of Marcabru's poems carries the line is itself unsettled: it is not the Spanish crusading song it is often credited to, and no critical edition was reachable to fix it.
suggested_refs: Gaunt, Harvey and Paterson, Marcabru: A Critical Edition, to settle which song carries the 'oltra mar' tornada

stops.name: Marseille, the port the sea story needs
stops.date_confidence: conjectural: Marseille is the principal southern-French embarkation port of the period, but no source names Rudel's port; the Provencal contingent under Alphonse Jourdain of Toulouse waited until August and crossed by sea, separately from the king's overland army
stops.campa: If Rudel sailed rather than marched, he sailed from here or from a harbor like it, in August, with the Provencal contingent that Alphonse Jourdain of Toulouse takes east by ship while the king's army is already deep in Hungary. No text names his port. This is the water Joffrey de Bourlemont will take ninety-two years later, aboard the ship of Thibaut of Navarre, a crusading king who composes songs on the crossing. The trope of the singing crusader is old before either of them uses it.
suggested_refs: The Provencal sea contingent of Alphonse Jourdain, August 1147
sources: General Second Crusade shipping patterns, Odo of Deuil at second hand

stops.name: Port-de-Bouc, the harbor named in the conditional
stops.date_confidence: hypothesis printed as hypothesis: French Wikipedia says 'Il se serait dans ce cas embarque a Port-de-Bouc', the conditional mood carrying the whole claim; the pool printed it as attested
stops.campa: One French account names a particular small harbor east of the Rhone mouth: he would in that case have embarked at Port-de-Bouc. The verb is in the conditional and the conditional is the entire content. The place makes its own first appearance in writing as Portus de Boc in this same year, 1147, which is a coincidence worth noticing and no kind of evidence. The reconstruction that puts him here also puts him in the king's Aquitanian company, and the king's company went overland; the two halves of the story cannot both stand.
suggested_refs: Port-de-Bouc, first attested as Portus de Boc in 1147

stops.name: Genoa, a leg that no text gives him
stops.date_confidence: conjectural: Genoese shipping carries much crusader traffic east in this period, but nothing places Rudel aboard any of it
stops.campa: Genoese hulls carry a large share of the traffic east in these years, and a ship out of Provence bound for the Levant may well put in here. This stop reconstructs a plausible stretch of a voyage that is itself only plausible. The honest description of the sea route is that the vida requires it, since the poet must fall ill aboard ship for the story to work, and that nothing outside the vida supports a single stage of it. The pins in this segment mark a hypothesis being followed to see where it goes.
suggested_refs: Genoese crusader shipping of the 1140s

stops.name: Messina, water and provisions
stops.date_confidence: conjectural: a standard waystation for Mediterranean crossings to Outremer, with no Rudel-specific attestation whatever
stops.campa: The strait is the ordinary halt on the run east: water, provisions, repairs, and news of what the weather is doing further on. Every western fleet bound for the Levant passes through here or around Sicily, and the Norman kings who hold the island make a business of the passing. If there was a ship with Rudel on it, it stopped somewhere like this. That sentence is the strongest thing that can be said, and it is a sentence about ships in general rather than about the man.
suggested_refs: Norman Sicily as waystation on the crusader sea route

stops.name: Limassol, a landfall out of its century
stops.date_confidence: anachronism, kept only as a flag: in 1148 Cyprus is Byzantine and Limassol a minor town; its harbor and merchant quarter date from Richard the Lionheart's conquest of 1191 and the three centuries of prosperity after it
stops.campa: The research pool called Cyprus the customary last landfall before the Levantine coast, and for the ships of the thirteenth century it is. In 1148 it is not. The island is Byzantine, Limassol is a small place, and its rise begins in 1191 when Richard the Lionheart takes Cyprus on his way to Acre and marries there. The stop stands as a correction rather than as an itinerary: this is what a later century's map does to an earlier century's voyage when nobody checks the dates.
suggested_refs: Limassol before 1191, and the Lusignan-era harbor that replaced it

stops.name: Constantinople, the other hypothesis passes through
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of the alternative route: the French host under Louis VII and Eleanor reaches Constantinople in autumn 1147; nothing places Rudel with it, and this hypothesis and the sea voyage cannot both be true
stops.campa: Louis VII, Eleanor, and the Aquitanian contingents come overland through Hungary and reach the walls of Constantinople in the autumn. Manuel Komnenos feeds them and hurries them across the Bosporus. If Rudel travels with the host to which his own lord's family belongs, his road runs here, and there is no ship, no shipboard illness, and no vida. The two reconstructions of his journey are mutually exclusive and both are unsupported. The sources do not choose, so the atlas does not choose for them.
suggested_refs: Odo of Deuil on the French army at Constantinople, autumn 1147
sources: Odo of Deuil, De profectione Ludovici VII, at second hand

stops.name: Mount Cadmus, the mountain that eats the army
stops.date_confidence: attested event, corrected coordinates: the disaster is 6 January 1148 in the mountains near Laodicea on the Lycus; the pool's pin lay 45 km east in open plain
stops.campa: The French column, strung out crossing the pass, is broken by Turkish attack; the vanguard has gone too far ahead, the baggage and the rear are cut to pieces, and Louis himself fights on foot with his back to a rock. Ephesus had already cost them in December. Whoever went east with this army in 1147 had a much better chance of dying on this slope than at any deathbed in a Lebanese port. If Rudel marched, he was here. No source names him among the present or the lost.
suggested_refs: The pass of Honaz Dagi near Laodicea, site of the disaster of 6 January 1148
sources: William of Tyre and Odo of Deuil, at second hand

stops.name: Antioch, where the pilgrims come from
stops.date_confidence: attested for the army: the remnant of Louis VII's force reaches Antioch on 19 March 1148, having taken ship at Attalia; Rudel's presence is not attested
stops.campa: What is left of the French army regroups at Antioch under Raymond of Poitiers, Eleanor's uncle, and the quarrel between king and queen that will end their marriage begins in this city. Antioch matters to the Rudel story for a different reason: the vida says the poet's love was kindled by pilgrims returning from Antioch who praised the countess of Tripoli to him. Men coming home from this city, in other words, are the mechanism by which a woman is said to have been described to a man who never saw her.
suggested_refs: Antioch in spring 1148, and the vida's pilgrims 'returning from Antioch'
sources: William of Tyre on the Antioch stage of the Second Crusade, at second hand

stops.name: Acre, the landing given in the conditional
stops.date_confidence: hypothesis, not record: French Wikipedia gives '13 avril 1148 a Saint-Jean-d'Acre' inside the same conditional sentence as Port-de-Bouc; it is incompatible with Louis VII's route through Antioch and fits only the Provencal sea contingent
stops.campa: A date and a harbor, precise to the day: the thirteenth of April, 1148, at Saint-Jean-d'Acre. It comes from the same conditional sentence as the departure from Port-de-Bouc, and precision of this kind in a hypothetical is a warning rather than a comfort. Seventy years later Francis of Assisi will come through this port on his way to the sultan's camp at Damietta, taking the same Provence-to-Levant water. Acre is where the west lands. Whether Rudel landed at all is the open question the date decorates.
suggested_refs: Saint-Jean-d'Acre as the port of entry to the Kingdom of Jerusalem

stops.name: Jerusalem, the city the vida never mentions
stops.date_confidence: gap, not itinerary: a pilgrimage to the Holy Sepulchre would be the natural discharge of a crusading vow, and the vida omits Jerusalem entirely, which is a hole in the story rather than evidence about it
stops.campa: A man who takes the cross goes to Jerusalem. That is what the vow is. Every crusader account in the corpus turns on this city, and the vida of Jaufre Rudel does not mention it once. Its poet crosses the sea for a woman and dies in a port two hundred miles north of the Holy Sepulchre, and the biography registers no lack. That silence is one of the clearest signs that the vida was written to explain poems rather than to record a journey: it keeps only what the songs require, and the songs require no Jerusalem.
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, absent from the vida of Jaufre Rudel
sources: Gap noted against the vida of Jaufre Rudel, which omits Jerusalem entirely

stops.name: Damascus, the siege that fails in four days
stops.date_confidence: attested for the expedition, not for Rudel: the council of Palmarea sends the host against Damascus in July 1148 and the siege collapses within days; no source places Rudel there, and the vida's chronology leaves little room for it
stops.campa: The council of Palmarea sends the assembled kings against Damascus, the one great Muslim city still friendly to the kingdom, and the siege falls apart in four days. The Second Crusade ends here, having accomplished nothing and lost a great deal. The vida gives Rudel a different July: a ship, a fever, a harbor in Tripoli. No source puts him under these walls. The two accounts of what a crusader did in the summer of 1148 do not overlap at any point, and only one of them was written by a poet.
suggested_refs: The siege of Damascus, July 1148, and the collapse of the Second Crusade
sources: William of Tyre, Historia rerum in partibus transmarinis gestarum, at second hand

segments.name: Tripoli, the Death in Her Arms

stops.name: Off Tripoli, the fever aboard ship
stops.date_confidence: tradition: the vida alone, written some seventy years later; no contemporary chronicle mentions the voyage, the illness, or the man
stops.campa: The vida says he falls gravely ill on the crossing and is taken for dead before the ship makes land. This is the Tripoli of Lebanon, the county's seat on its hill above the sea, five hundred years after Marina the Monk grew up in a village along this same coast at Al-Qalamoun. It is not the Tripolitania that Emin Arslan wrote of from Buenos Aires seven centuries later; the name collides and the places do not. The distinction matters because the legend has been pinned to the wrong shore more than once.
suggested_refs: The sea approach to Crusader-era Tripoli

stops.name: El Mina, carried ashore as if dead
stops.date_confidence: tradition, with topography inferred: the vida says he was carried to a lodging at Tripoli, and El Mina is the working harbor where a ship would actually land, below the hill town
stops.campa: The harbor quarter lies on the shore, a mile or so from the citadel on its hill. A ship coming in makes land here, and the sick man is carried up to a lodging and laid down in it, believed to be dying. The vida gives no name to the house, to the ship, or to anyone who carried him. What it gives instead is a shape: the far love has to be approached by water, and the lover has to be nearly dead on arrival, or the poems it was written to explain would not make the sense it wants them to make.
suggested_refs: El Mina, the harbor quarter of Crusader-era Tripoli
sources: Vida of Jaufre Rudel; historical topography of Crusader-era Tripoli

stops.name: Tripoli, the countess comes down from the citadel
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and English-language scholarship calls it likely fictional, 'derived from the enigmatic nature of Rudel's verse'; no contemporary chronicle corroborates the meeting or the deathbed
stops.campa: They tell the countess that a stranger is dying in the town below who loves her and has never seen her. She comes down to the lodging and takes him in her arms. He recovers his senses long enough to know who is holding him, and dies. The vida never gives her a personal name; she is la comtessa de Tripol and nothing more. Later readers supply Hodierna, or her daughter Melisende, or both in turn. Every retelling since works from this scene, and no record outside this one text says it happened.
stops.quote: Él enfermó estando en la nave, y fue llevado a Trípoli, a un albergue y tenido por muerto. Se lo hicieron saber a la Condesa; y ella fue a él, hasta su lecho y lo tomó entre sus brazos.
stops.quote_source: Vida of Jaufre Rudel, death scene in the Spanish rendering printed in the Spanish Wikipedia article 'Jaufré Rudel'; translator uncredited, Occitan original not reproduced there
suggested_refs: The vida's death scene, and the modern scholarly judgement that it is a construction from the verse

stops.name: Tripoli, buried in the house of the Temple
stops.date_confidence: tradition: the vida says she buried him with great honor 'en la maion del Temple'; the Templars did hold property in Tripoli through the twelfth century, but no building, tomb, or inscription there has ever been linked to Rudel
stops.campa: The countess has him buried honorably in the house of the Temple. The Templars do hold property in the city through this century, so the detail is not impossible, and that is the whole of what can be said for it. Nothing has ever been found: no tomb, no stone, no inscription, no notice in any Tripolitan record. A hundred and fifty years later Jacques de Molay will be the last master of the order that is said to have taken this body in, and the Temple will have no house in Tripoli or anywhere else.
suggested_refs: Templar property in twelfth-century Tripoli; no surviving trace of the burial

stops.name: Tripoli, the veil taken the same day
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and the weakest part of it: no source names the house she is said to have entered, and modern philology treats the closing scene as embellishment added to complete the poem's logic
stops.campa: The vida closes with the countess entering a convent that same day. No source names the house. The historical Hodierna does nothing of the kind: she is countess for another four years, then regent of Tripoli for three more, and dies on a twenty-first of December whose year nobody wrote down. The ending is there because the story needs the woman to be as unavailable after the meeting as she was before it. Far love must stay far, and a veil is the only way to keep it so once she has been seen.
suggested_refs: The unnamed convent of the vida's coda, unlocated in every source
sources: Alfred Jeanroy, Les chansons de Jaufre Rudel (1915), at second hand

stops.name: Tripoli, the widow governs
stops.date_confidence: attested: Raymond II is killed in 1152 and Hodierna rules as regent for her minor son Raymond III
stops.campa: Raymond II is killed and Hodierna takes the county in her own hands, regent for a son who is twelve. She governs Tripoli for three years, in the same rooms on the same hill where the vida had put her four years earlier, weeping over a dead Frenchman and taking the veil. She does neither. She holds a frontier state between Antioch and the kingdom, and the record of her that survives is administrative: attendances, charters, a regency, the ordinary paperwork of rule.
suggested_refs: The regency of Hodierna for Raymond III, 1152 to 1155

stops.name: Tripoli, the regency ends
stops.date_confidence: attested: the regency ends in 1155 when Raymond III comes of age
stops.campa: Raymond III comes of age and takes the county. His mother steps back into the position the sources have no vocabulary for, dowager countess of a small state, sister of the queen of Jerusalem, present at courts and named in acts. Her son will be captured by Nur ad-Din and spend eight years in a Muslim prison, and will govern the kingdom itself as regent afterward. None of this reaches the poem. The Occitan tradition wants only her title and the fact that Tripoli is far from Blaye.
suggested_refs: Raymond III of Tripoli, count from 1155

stops.name: Tripoli, a day without a year
stops.date_confidence: only the day is attested: the source states that 'the year and cause of her death are not recorded'; Melisende died 11 September 1161, roughly three months earlier, and c.1161 or c.1162 is reconstruction
stops.campa: Hodierna dies on the twenty-first of December. The day is recorded and the year is not, which is an exact inversion of her afterlife, where the year 1148 is fixed to the hour of her legend and the woman herself has no biography at all. Her sister Melisende, queen of Jerusalem, had died about three months before. She is somewhere between forty-five and forty-seven. The countess of Tripoli of the poem has by now been dead for fourteen years in a story that had not yet been written.
suggested_refs: The death notice of Hodierna, 21 December, year unrecorded

stops.name: Ruad, the last island off the same coast
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fall of Ruad, 1302; included as the closing of the Frankish Levant, not as an event in Rudel's life
stops.campa: Tripoli falls to the Mamluks in 1289. Thirteen years later the last Templar garrison in the east, holding the little island of Ruad off this coast, is taken by a fleet sailing out of Tripoli harbor, and Jacques de Molay loses the final foothold of the order that is said to have buried a poet in its house down the shore. The county of the countess is gone. What survives of the whole crusader Levant, in Occitan letters, is a love story about a woman who is not named and a man who may never have arrived.
suggested_refs: The fall of Ruad, 1302, last Templar position in the Levant

segments.name: The Vida and Its Long Afterlife

stops.name: Treviso, the biography is written
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the vidas are generally dated to the second quarter of the thirteenth century, German scholarship putting Uc de Saint Circ's biographies around 1225; the pool's flat 1250 is the far end of a c.1225 to 1250 bracket
stops.campa: At the courts of the da Romano family in the Veneto, an exiled troubadour from Quercy called Uc de Saint Circ writes prose lives for the poets whose songs he has collected. The vida of Jaufre Rudel is one of them: eleven or twelve lines, written some seventy years after the man died, by someone with the poems in front of him and no other source. This is the whole origin of the story. Dante will move through these same northern courts a lifetime later and set Arnaut Daniel among the purified poets of love.
stops.quote: Jaufres Rudels de Blaia si fo mout gentils om, princes de Blaia
stops.quote_source: Anonymous thirteenth-century vida of Jaufre Rudel, Occitan, opening sentence, as quoted in the French Wikipedia article 'Jaufré Rudel'; the Italian article gives 'hom' for 'om' and continues 'Et enamoret se de la comtessa de Tripol'
suggested_refs: Boutiere and Schutz, Biographies des troubadours, on the attribution of the vidas to Uc de Saint Circ

stops.name: Paris, the manuscripts at Richelieu
stops.date_confidence: attested for the manuscripts, approximate for the copying date: the chansonniers are thirteenth-century copies made in Italy and southern France; the pin is the Departement des Manuscrits at Richelieu, not the Tolbiac site the pool gave
stops.campa: Everything that survives of Jaufre Rudel is in two codices and their relatives: BnF fr. 854 and fr. 12473, Occitan chansonniers copied in Italy and southern France about a century after his death. Chansonnier K carries a miniature of him on horseback, which is a thirteenth-century illuminator's idea of a twelfth-century lord and not a portrait. Nothing in his hand exists. The poems, the melodies, the vida, and the face are all one hundred years downstream of the man, in one library, on the rue de Richelieu.
suggested_refs: BnF fr. 854 and fr. 12473, Chansonniers provencaux I and K, Departement des Manuscrits

stops.name: Arqua Petrarca, the legend enters Italian
stops.date_confidence: attested that Petrarch names Rudel in the Triumphus Cupidinis; the exact wording is not printed here because the line the pool supplied is prose and appears in no edition reached, and the standard reading could not be checked against a critical edition
stops.campa: In the hills south of Padua, Petrarch writes the Trionfi and puts Rudel in the catalogue of Love's captives: the man of Blaye who used sail and oar to go looking for his own death. The line carries the legend out of Occitan and into the language that will keep it. Its exact words are not reproduced here. What circulates as the quotation is prose, not terza rima, and no critical edition was reachable to establish the reading, so the atlas records that Petrarch named him and refuses to put words in his mouth.
suggested_refs: Petrarch, Triumphus Cupidinis IV, the troubadour catalogue, in a critical edition
sources: Petrarch, Trionfi, reported at second hand; wording unverified and therefore unquoted

stops.name: Maillane, Mistral gives her the wrong name
stops.date_confidence: attested publication, chronologically impossible identification: Melisende of Tripoli is Hodierna's daughter, born after Rudel's presumed death; the entry is nineteenth-century Provencal local tradition, not evidence about the 1140s
stops.campa: Frederic Mistral, compiling the great Provencal dictionary at Maillane, enters the countess under the daughter's name rather than the mother's. Melisende of Tripoli was born after Rudel was dead, so the identification cannot stand as history, and as legend it is now the dominant one. This is the Provence of the gaya ciencia that Yolande of Aragon summered in at Tarascon four centuries earlier, reviving itself in the nineteenth century and rewriting its own medieval material as it goes.
stops.quote: Mélisende, Mélissande or Mélissène, countess of Tripoli, daughter of Aimeri de Lusignan, loved by the troubadour Geoffroi Rudel
stops.quote_source: Frederic Mistral, Lou Tresor dou Felibrige (1878), entry on Melisende, in the English translation quoted in the English Wikipedia article 'Jaufre Rudel'; Mistral's own French and Provencal wording not checked
suggested_refs: Lou Tresor dou Felibrige (1878), entry on Melisende

stops.name: Paris, the distant princess on stage
stops.date_confidence: attested: premiere at the Theatre de la Renaissance, 5 April 1895
stops.campa: Edmond Rostand's La Princesse lointaine opens at the Theatre de la Renaissance with Sarah Bernhardt as the countess, renamed Melisandre after Mistral's version. The verse play, not the medieval vida, is where nearly every modern retelling of Rudel comes from. Bernhardt takes it to London the same year, where George Bernard Shaw, who wants realism, dislikes it thoroughly. A dying poet, a woman he has never seen, a ship: the nineteenth century finds in the twelfth exactly what it went looking for.
suggested_refs: Edmond Rostand, La Princesse lointaine (1895), and the Bernhardt production

stops.name: Salzburg, the far love set to music
stops.date_confidence: attested premiere at the Salzburg Festival in 2000; the exact festival date was not in the verified pool and the day defaults
stops.campa: Kaija Saariaho and Amin Maalouf make an opera of it: L'Amour de loin, the poet, the countess, and a pilgrim who carries word between them across the water. It premieres at the Salzburg Festival and reaches Santa Fe two years later. A Finnish composer and a Lebanese writer, between them, return the story to the two coasts it belongs to. Eight hundred and fifty years after the vida, the working parts are unchanged: distance, hearsay, a sea crossing, and a woman described to a man who cannot verify the description.
suggested_refs: Kaija Saariaho and Amin Maalouf, L'Amour de loin, Salzburg 2000 and Santa Fe 2002

stops.name: Blaye, the town keeps the name
stops.date_confidence: attested: the micronation Helianthis was founded in 2013 in homage to the principality of Blaye and to Rudel; the street and school namings are undated in the sources
stops.campa: Streets carry his name at Blaye, Bruges, Montpellier and Toulouse, a lycee at Blaye is named for him, and in 2013 a micronation called Helianthis is declared in homage to the seigneurial principality of Blaye and its poet. In 2020 Francis Cabrel names him in a song about the rockstars of the Middle Ages. The town has no tomb and no contemporary monument to the man. What it has is the phrase he wrote, amor de lonh, and everything nine centuries have built on top of it.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Jaufre Rudel at Blaye, and the 2013 micronation of Helianthis
